description: We are Team Cyone, a group of enthusiastic students passionate about space exploration, technology, and innovation. We are participating in the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 to develop creative, data-driven solutions to real-world space exploration challenges. Our interests include software development, AI, data analysis, and scientific research. We believe in teamwork, creativity, and learning together as we explore new possibilities beyond Earth.
summary:
LUNA-NAV (Lunar Landing Site & Operations Navigator) is an interactive lunar mission-planning and educational platform that makes complex lunar exploration more accessible.

Unexpected launch delays can change sunlight availability, Earth visibility, and operational conditions, requiring mission planners to reassess landing sites and mission dates.

Using NASA lunar elevation data and astronomical calculations, LUNA-NAV allows users to compare landing sites and schedules, customize solar-array configurations, estimate power generation, assess thermal hazards, and explore Earth communication windows.

Interactive 3D lunar terrain, synchronized timelines, and side-by-side comparisons help users understand how engineering decisions affect mission feasibility.

Beyond researchers and mission planners, educators can demonstrate lunar science, students can experiment with real mission scenarios, and the general public can explore and learn about lunar operations without requiring specialist knowledge.

By integrating these capabilities into one user-friendly platform, LUNA-NAV supports both early-stage mission analysis and accessible space education.
details:
LUNA-NAV — Lunar Landing Site & Operations Navigator

What We Built

LUNA-NAV is a full-stack lunar mission-planning and educational platform developed by Team Cyone for NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026.

Lunar landing missions are planned around carefully selected dates, locations, and operational conditions. Unexpected launch delays can change sunlight availability and Earth communication opportunities, requiring mission teams to reassess their plans.

LUNA-NAV addresses this challenge by allowing users to explore alternative landing sites, change mission schedules, adjust selected spacecraft configurations, and compare the resulting operational conditions in one interactive environment.

How It Works

LUNA-NAV uses a React and TypeScript frontend with a Python FastAPI scientific backend.

The backend processes lunar elevation information to construct local digital elevation models and calculate 360-degree terrain-horizon profiles. These calculations account for surrounding obstacles and lunar curvature.

Sun and Earth positions are calculated for selected mission dates and compared with the terrain horizon to estimate solar illumination and potential direct-to-Earth communication.

A time-series evaluation produces mission metrics including sunlight availability, continuous darkness, solar power, communication windows, and an estimated composite viability score.

The frontend presents these results through interactive 3D terrain visualization, polar sky charts, operational timelines, and scenario-comparison dashboards.

Engineering Features

Launch-Delay and Multi-Site Comparison: Users can adjust mission dates and compare alternative landing locations when the original schedule changes.

Hardware-Aware Solar Analysis: Different solar-array configurations experience different sunlight incidence. LUNA-NAV models vertical, horizontal, and Sun-tracking configurations, allowing users to examine their estimated performance.

Adjustable Solar Power: Users can change solar-panel area and explore its effect on estimated electrical generation.

Thermal and Cryogenic Risk Assessment: A simplified temperature model informed by lunar thermal conditions highlights potentially hazardous cold regions and extreme-temperature exposure. This supports thermal-risk exploration without claiming to predict actual internal spacecraft temperatures.

Direct-to-Earth Communication Windows: Users can change the minimum clearance angle above the local terrain horizon and evaluate how it affects potential Earth-visibility windows.

Interactive Lunar Education: Guided tutorials, scientific visualizations, and mission controls help educators, students, and the general public understand lunar exploration without requiring specialist software expertise.

NASA Data and Scientific Methods

The project integrates NASA LOLA digital elevation processing, astronomical ephemeris calculations, and lunar surface visualization resources.

Its terrain pipeline supports georeferenced LOLA GeoTIFF extraction and a fallback terrain representation when the primary raster cannot be used.

NASA JPL Horizons is incorporated for Sun and Earth position calculations and astronomical reference comparisons, with a local ephemeris fallback where necessary.

The application also uses simplified thermal and surface-appearance models informed by lunar exploration datasets.

What Makes LUNA-NAV Different

Existing tools provide valuable lunar mapping, astronomical and engineering information.

LUNA-NAV focuses on combining these related decisions into an accessible mission trade-study workflow.

Users can explore how changing a launch date, landing location, solar-array configuration, panel area, or communication-clearance requirement affects the resulting operational scenario.

Rather than displaying isolated measurements, LUNA-NAV helps users understand the relationships between mission decisions and their consequences.

Benefits and Impact

Mission researchers and engineers can use LUNA-NAV to investigate alternative operational scenarios during early-stage mission planning.

Educators can demonstrate lunar terrain, illumination, communication geometry, and energy considerations interactively.

Students and the general public can explore real lunar science concepts, test mission assumptions, and understand why selecting a lunar landing site is a complex engineering decision.

The platform aims to make lunar mission trade studies more accessible while encouraging scientific understanding and informed decision-making.

Technologies Used

Frontend: React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Three.js, React Three Fiber, Recharts, and SVG visualization.

Backend: Python, FastAPI, Uvicorn, Pydantic, NumPy, SciPy, Skyfield, Rasterio, Pillow, and Requests.

Scientific processing: Lunar coordinate transformations, topocentric Sun and Earth calculations, DEM-based horizon analysis, illumination modeling, solar-power estimation, and comparative mission metrics.

Limitations and Future Development

LUNA-NAV is an early-stage scientific decision-support and educational prototype, not a flight-certified mission-planning system.

Model limitations include terrain resolution, data availability, simplified thermal assumptions, spacecraft power-model approximations, and the absence of comprehensive communication link-budget analysis.

Future development will focus on improved terrain accuracy, stronger independent scientific validation, more detailed thermal and energy models, and additional mission-planning capabilities.

Our goal is to make lunar exploration easier to understand and mission alternatives easier to evaluate.
